parts.title: Giving a Computer Model a Head Start on Reaching Helps Its Brain Activity Match the Real Motor Cortex
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Scientists who study how the brain controls movement often use a kind of computer model called a recurrent neural network, or RNN. An RNN is a network of artificial neurons that keeps a running memory of what has happened so far. Researchers train these networks to do a particular task, such as reaching for a target, and then compare the network's activity with recordings from the motor cortex, the part of the brain that plans and sends out movements. The usual assumption is that, because the network and the brain both solve the same task, the network has learned the same underlying ways of computing as the brain's own nerve circuits.

The brain, however, is wired in a very specific and highly organized way. As an animal grows up, its motor cortex also builds up a rich set of basic movement skills, called motor primitives, by learning to control its body over and over. Most task-trained RNNs start from random settings and are trained straight away on one specific task. So a key question remains: how much can these models really tell us about the motor cortex?

In this study, we propose a way to model the motor cortex that first gives the network a head start, or pretraining, on a single reaching skill. Our RNN receives sensory feedback (what the arm is doing) and task instructions. It then produces movement commands that drive a computer model of an arm with muscles and joints. Before any task training, this model can reach from any point to any other point in its workspace, following a smooth, natural path known as a minimum-jerk trajectory.

We compared this pre-trained model with models trained directly on particular tasks. In two tasks, the center-out (CO) task and the random target touch (RTT) task, the pre-trained model's activity matched real neural recordings more closely. This was true both in the pattern of which states the network visits (its neural geometry) and in how its activity changes over time (its neural dynamics). Surprisingly, we saw the opposite pattern in a double-reach (DR) task. In this task, two targets appear at the same time, rather than the next target appearing only after the previous movement is finished, as in the RTT task. This suggests that the brain plans a series of movements as one joined-up unit, and that this ability may be built into the circuits of the motor cortex.

In summary, our results suggest that giving a network abilities beyond what the immediate task requires, through more systematic training or other methods, can help us better understand how the brain's own nerve circuits work.

Keywords: motor control, motor primitive, recurrent neural network, musculoskeletal arm model, neural population dynamics
parts.introduction_first: Controlling movement is one of the most basic things animals do, and it has long been a central topic in neuroscience. In the past, researchers trained animals to perform particular movement tasks. While the animals did so, they recorded the activity of nerve cells in the motor cortex, the brain region that plans and sends out movements, using electrodes placed inside the brain [1,2,3,4,5,6]. In recent years, new technology has made it possible to record from very large numbers of nerve cells at once. This has shifted attention away from single nerve cells and toward how whole groups of them work together [7,8,9,10,11]. As a result, the main way of making sense of motor cortex activity is now to treat it as a dynamical system: a set of rules that describe how the activity changes over time [12,13,14,15,16]. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are computer models that keep a running memory of what has happened so far, so they are dynamical systems by nature. This has made them powerful tools for modeling the brain in this setting [17,18]. They have helped researchers understand how the brain's calculations depend on context [19], how it produces muscle activity [20], how it uses basic movement building blocks called motor primitives [21], and how it prepares for movement [22].
parts.conclusion:
5. Conclusions

In this work, we propose a promising design that combines pretraining with RNN models that control a simulated body. This opens up several new directions for research. One is to give the pretraining richer experiences that draw on more than one sense. Another is to combine pretraining, where the network learns from correct answers, with reinforcement learning, where it learns by trial and error from rewards. A third is to use pre-trained networks as computer testbeds for brain–machine interface methods, the techniques that turn brain signals into commands for devices. By giving RNNs realistic experience of sensing and moving, we move toward models that not only perform tasks but also explain how the brain's nerve circuits solve problems. This is a crucial step toward building theories of how the brain works that are grounded in the rules of computing.
parts.introduction_rest:
Researchers use RNNs to model the brain's nerve networks in two broad ways. The first is data-driven modeling [23,24]. Here, the network is adjusted until its activity closely matches the activity actually recorded from the brain. These models are very good at reproducing the recordings. But they can only describe what the activity looks like. They cannot show why particular patterns of activity appear, or how the demands of a task shape those patterns. The second is task-driven modeling [20,25], which is now the more common approach. In this approach, the network's connections are trained using the conditions of a task from animal experiments. The network takes the task conditions as input and produces the animal's movement or target as output. The trained model is then compared with the recorded brain activity, either for single nerve cells or for groups of them [26,27]. The aim is to work out the ways of computing that the animal uses to perform the same task [28,29,30].

Task-driven modeling rests on a central assumption. If a network solves the same task as an animal and reproduces the animal's patterns of activity, then the two may be using similar ways of computing underneath. Recent findings have challenged this assumption. Researchers found that many different networks can solve the same task, a property called solution degeneracy. When networks are trained on the same task but start from different random settings, they end up with quite different patterns of activity, and only some of these match the brain recordings [31]. This happens precisely because networks that start from random settings lack the organized starting point that the brain's circuits gain through evolution and development.

The brain, by contrast, is already wired in a highly optimized way when an animal is born [32]. Over millions of years of evolution, and over the years of sensing and moving that an animal goes through as it grows up, the motor cortex builds up a rich and flexible set of basic movement skills. So when an animal that has never been trained before meets a new task in the laboratory, it already has a foundation of movement abilities. Its learning is basically about using these existing skills to work out the rules of the task.

This idea fits with a growing body of work on pretraining in computational neuroscience, the study of how the brain works using computer models. One kind of pretraining, called compositional pretraining, trains a network on the smaller building blocks of a task before it learns the full task. This makes the network more efficient and helps it match animal behavior on complex thinking tasks [33]. In another study, mice were trained without any correct answers being shown them, a method called unsupervised pretraining, on the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes what they see. This produced patterns of activity that made later learning faster, giving direct biological evidence that the brain uses pretraining-like mechanisms [34]. A third study found that a warm-up period of training with random noise helps a network judge how uncertain it is about its answers. This mirrors the role of spontaneous activity, the brain's own background activity, in developing circuits [35]. Finally, starting a network with connections arranged to resemble the brain's own wiring greatly improves how well an RNN matches the motor cortex [32]. Together, these studies suggest that how a network is started and pre-trained may matter as much as its design in deciding how it computes. However, as far as we know, no earlier study has carefully tested whether pretraining on a wide range of movement skills, rather than on single thinking tasks or on random noise, can close the gap between the activity of artificial RNNs and the activity of the motor cortex.

At the same time, studies of controlling a simulated body have shown that movement control cannot be understood apart from the body being controlled. Researchers have built computer models of muscles and joints that can be trained by adjusting their settings step by step, such as MotorNet [36] and μSim [37]. These have made it possible to train whole neural controllers, from start to finish, that drive realistic arms and other body parts. Such studies have shown that including the physics of muscles and joints changes the kind of control a network learns. For example, networks controlling an arm show different patterns of activity than networks controlling an eye [38]. Sensory feedback from the body [39,40] or task instructions [41] also shape the network's internal patterns of activity in ways that do not appear in models that only track movement. Despite this progress, most studies of simulated bodies still train their controllers from random settings on a single target task. This is very different from how the brain develops: the motor circuits are shaped by many kinds of sensing and moving before the animal ever meets a particular experimental task [42,43].

To explore this question, we first ask what happens when animals are trained on a variety of movement tasks. Take the macaque monkey as an example. Whatever the task, doing it well requires the monkey to already have a movement ability: reaching, which it has already learned. So the whole training process can be seen as the monkey fitting the task's rule into its own system of sensing and moving, which broadly includes its thinking system too. As a result, the activity patterns we see in the trained monkey's motor cortex probably reflect some kind of blend between two things: the task's rule as it is carried out in the motor regions, and the motor system's own natural patterns of activity (shown in Figure 1). We therefore built a series of models to simulate this situation as faithfully as possible, and tested them on several classic tasks from the field of movement control.

To measure how similar a model's activity is to the brain's activity, we need measures that work at two levels. The first level is the pattern of which states the network visits, known as its neural geometry. Here, a method called canonical correlation analysis (CCA) is used on the network's activity after it has been reduced to a few main directions of change. CCA checks whether the model and the brain pass through similar states while the animal behaves [44]. The second level is the pattern of how activity changes over time, known as its neural dynamics. This asks not only which states are visited but also how the system moves from one state to the next. A method called dynamical similarity analysis (DSA) adds to CCA here. It compares mathematical descriptions of how each system changes over time, called Koopman operators, after lining the two systems up as closely as possible. This gives a distance measure that captures whether the two systems follow the same kind of flow, a property called topological conjugacy [45]. Recent work has shown that these two levels can come apart: two systems may visit similar states while following fundamentally different rules [30]. This is why we use both measures to judge how well a model matches the brain.

In this work, we bring these threads together by proposing a third approach, which we call developmental pretraining, that is fundamentally different from both earlier approaches. Unlike data-driven models, our model is never directly trained on brain recordings. Instead, brain-like activity emerges as a side effect of the model learning a wide range of behaviors by interacting with its simulated body. Standard task-driven models start from random settings and are trained from scratch on a single, narrow task. Our model, by contrast, first learns a varied set of reaching skills across a whole workspace, simulating how the brain acquires basic movement skills as it develops. We then tested the model systematically using CCA and DSA. Our aim was to find out how pretraining, within a setup where the network controls a simulated arm with muscles and joints, affects how well it matches recordings from the motor cortex of monkeys across several kinds of task.

There is also evidence from studies of the brain that suggests a series of reaching tasks is planned as one joined-up whole, rather than as a chain of separate pieces [46,47]. This may depend on processes that unfold over several different time scales [48], on metastable attractors, which are states the brain tends to settle into for a while before switching to another [49], or on loops between the thalamus, a relay station in the brain, and the cortex [50]. To take our investigation further, in the final part we examined whether a single reach and a double reach rely on fundamentally different ways of computing.
parts.methods:
2. Materials and Methods

2.1. How the Model Is Built

We built our computer model (Figure 2A) with the biological system shown in Figure 1 in mind. At its heart is a recurrent neural network (RNN) that stands in for the motor cortex. The RNN's outputs drive a computer model of an arm with muscles and joints, which moves in a flat, two-dimensional plane. The arm has two links, a shoulder and an elbow, and it carries out reaching movements.

The inputs that belong to the task are handled by a separate part of the model, which we call the task network. Together with visual feedback and proprioceptive feedback (the sense of where the body's own parts are), these inputs pass into the RNN through an input layer. In the sections below, we describe each of these parts in detail.

Figure 2

How the model is built and how it is trained. (A) The main model has three connected parts: an RNN controller, a task network (Task net), and a computer model of an arm with muscles and joints. The task inputs, a "hold" signal and the target location, pass through the task network to the RNN. The RNN then produces actions that drive the arm, so that the tip of the arm follows the planned path and speed. (B) At first, all the network's settings are trained together on a grid of reaching points, which gives the model a basic reaching skill. (C) For the later tasks, all the internal recurrent weights inside the RNN are frozen (kept fixed), so only the task network's settings can be trained.

2.1.1. The RNN Controller

We wanted the model to reflect key principles of how the brain's nerve circuits are organized, while still being flexible enough to learn complex tasks. So we built an excitatory–inhibitory recurrent neural network that runs in continuous time, meaning it changes smoothly rather than in separate steps. It also follows several rules that are thought to be realistic for the brain [25].

The network had N = 100 neurons. Of these, 80% were excitatory (Ne = 0.8N), which push other neurons toward firing, and 20% were inhibitory (Ni = 0.2N), which push them away. This split follows Dale's law, a rule in the brain that each neuron tends to send either excitatory or inhibitory signals. Each neuron was treated as a hidden unit, a unit whose activity is not directly observed. Every unit had the same fixed time constant τ = 50 ms, which sets how quickly it responds to changes. The network's hidden state h(t), a list of N numbers that holds its running memory, changed over time according to

(1) τ dh(t)/dt = −h(t) + f(Wrec h(t) + Win u(t) + b) + 2τσrec ξrec(t),

where Wrec ∈ R^(N×N) is the recurrent weight matrix, the table of numbers that sets how strongly each neuron affects each other neuron. Win ∈ R^(N×M) is the input weight matrix, with M = 26, the total number of inputs. The input u(t) is the list of inputs, which changes over time. The bias b ∈ R^N is a fixed offset. The activation function f(·) is tanh(·), a smooth function that squeezes values into the range (−1, 1). During training, ξrec(t) is Gaussian noise, random jitter drawn from a bell-shaped curve, with a standard deviation of σrec = 0.15. This noise helps the network learn in a robust way.

In practice, a computer cannot run continuous time, so we used the Euler method to break time into steps of Δt = 10 ms. This gives the update rule

(2) h_(t+1) = (1 − α) h_t + α · f(Wrec h_t + Win u_t + b) + 2τσrec ξrec(t), α = Δt/τ.

The network's output came from a linear readout layer followed by a sigmoid function σ(·), which squeezes values into the range (0, 1):

(3) y_t = σ(Wout h_t + bout).

Here Wout ∈ R^(6×N) is the output weight matrix, and bout ∈ R^6 is a constant bias.

2.1.2. The Arm Model

To better imitate how the brain controls arm movements, we used the RNN controller to drive a computer model of an arm with muscles and joints. We used the PyTorch version of MotorNet (Version 0.2.0) [36], a recently developed simulation toolbox for such systems. It offers many ready-made skeletal models, muscle models, and complete arm assemblies. We chose the RigidTendonArm26 arm, which moves in a flat plane and has two joints. It is powered by six RigidTendonHillMuscle actuators: a shoulder flexor (SF), a shoulder extensor (SE), an elbow flexor (EF), an elbow extensor (EE), a bi-articular flexor (BF), and a bi-articular extensor (BE). A bi-articular muscle crosses two joints. This model gives a realistic platform for simulating human upper-limb movements.

All models in MotorNet inherit from PyTorch's nn.Module. When we give the model the muscle activations, it automatically works out the forward dynamics and kinematics of the muscles and skeleton. In other words, it calculates how the forces produce movement and how the arm's parts move as a result. It then reports movement details such as the position and speed of the arm tip, the joint angles and their speeds, the muscle length, how fast the muscle is shortening, and the muscle force.

Importantly, the model is fully differentiable. This means it can take part in backpropagation, the process by which a network works out how each of its settings contributed to an error. As a result, the model's outputs can be fed straight into the loss function, the score that training tries to make as small as possible. This makes end-to-end learning much easier.

To make the model easy to use, MotorNet also provides an Environment class. It joins the arm model with the task rules and the sensory observation steps, so users can freely choose what goes in and what comes out and can add noise of their own. In our setup, sensory feedback was the position of the arm tip (visual feedback) and the muscle length and shortening speed (proprioceptive feedback). Together with the task inputs (described below), these formed the observation vector. The outputs were the arm tip's position, its speed, and the muscle forces. During training, both the visual and proprioceptive feedback delays were set to 0 ms, and the noise level was fixed at 0.10. During testing, the noise was set to 0.

2.1.3. What the RNN and Task Network Receive

The input vector u(t) had two main parts: sensory feedback and task instructions:

(4) u_t = [fb_t, task_output_t].

As Section 2.1.2 described, the sensory feedback was the arm tip's position (2 numbers) and the muscle length and shortening speed (6 muscles × 2 = 12 numbers). The task part was produced by a separate feedforward network, the task network (tasknet). A feedforward network passes information forward without any loops. It took the abstract task instructions, task_input_t, and produced four numbers in most cases: the target position, the motor vigor (how strongly the arm should move), and the hold signal:

(5) task_output_t = g_θtask(task_input_t),

where g(·) is a multi-layer perceptron, a simple stack of layers of neurons, with a tanh activation function. This design lets the RNN receive high-level, processed inputs (12 numbers in most cases) rather than raw instructions. Table 1 shows all the network settings.

Table 1

|---|---|---|---|
| Task Network | Linear + Tanh | 4 (or 6) a | 64 |
| | Linear | 64 | 12 |
| Input Layer | Sensory feedback (FB) | 14 b | – |

| Recurrent Layer | Linear (no bias) | 100 | 100 |

2.1.4. Starting Values for the Network

We set the starting values of all the network's settings as follows.

Recurrent weights: The recurrent weight matrix Wrec follows a structured excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) pattern:

Wrec = [ WEE  −WEI ; WIE  −WII ] ∈ R^(N×N)

where all four blocks, WEE ∈ R^(Ne×Ne), WEI ∈ R^(Ne×Ni), WIE ∈ R^(Ni×Ne), and WII ∈ R^(Ni×Ni), start with non-negative numbers.

We set the average (mean) and spread (variance) of the weights so that the network starts in a balanced state:

μE = 1/N, mean for excitatory connections; μI = Ne/Ni N, mean for inhibitory connections; σ² = 1/N, variance for all connections

Each connection is drawn from a normal (bell-shaped) distribution, w_ij ∼ N(μ, σ²), with the right μ depending on the type of connection (E→E, E→I, I→E, I→I).

To keep the network's activity stable, we scaled the recurrent weight matrix so that its spectral radius r = 1.5. The spectral radius is the largest size of the matrix's eigenvalues, which roughly tells us how strongly the network's activity can grow:

Wrec ← r/ρ(Wrec) · Wrec

where ρ(Wrec) = max_i |λ_i(Wrec)| is the spectral radius of the weight matrix.

Input weights: The input weight matrix Win ∈ R^(N×M) starts with excitatory connections only: Win ∼ N(μE, σ²).

Output weights: The output weight matrix Wout ∈ R^(6×N) connects only to excitatory neurons: Wout[:,1:Ne] ∼ N(μE, σ²), Wout[:,Ne+1:]=0.

Bias: The recurrent layer bias brec starts at 0, and the output layer bias bout ∈ R^P starts at 0.6.

Initial state: The network's starting hidden state was drawn from a Gaussian distribution with an average of 0 and a small variance: h0 ∼ N(0, σ0² I), σ0 = 0.1.

2.2. The Tasks and How We Trained the Model

2.2.1. Movement Path and Speed

To make the movement paths look more like those of humans or animals, we used the minimum-jerk trajectory model. Proposed by Flash and Hogan [51], this model produces smooth reaching movements by making the jerk as small as possible over the whole movement. Jerk is how quickly acceleration changes. In mathematical terms, it minimizes the time integral of the squared jerk.

Given a starting hand position H1 = (x1, y1), a target position H2 = (x2, y2), and a movement duration t, we describe the path using normalized time τ, which runs from 0 to 1:

(6) τ = T/t, T ∈ [0, t]

The hand position at normalized time follows a fifth-order polynomial, a smooth curve built from powers up to τ^5:

(7) H(τ) = H1 + (H1 − H2) · (15τ^4 − 6τ^5 − 10τ^3)

The speed profile comes from differentiating the position equation with respect to real time T:

(8) Ḣ(T) = (H1 − H2) · (−30T^4/t^5 + 60T^3/t^4 − 30T^2/t^3)

2.2.2. The Grid Task

The main goal of this study is to give an RNN the ability to control an arm model and drive its forward dynamics. In other words, given a target point, the RNN should be able to guide the arm tip from any starting position to that target along a minimum-jerk path. To do this, the network must learn a huge range of point-to-point reaches. Our main approach was to create a set of grid points. Each point served as a starting location, and every other point served as a target. This trained the network to move between any pair of points in the grid.

Joint-Space Grid Points: We created points from the two joint angles of the two-jointed arm. The upper arm angle relative to the shoulder is θ1 (0° < θ1 < 140°), and the forearm angle at the elbow is θ2 (0° < θ2 < 160°). The arm tip's position in joint space is written as (θ1, θ2). We picked values of θ1 and θ2 at fixed steps Δθ, that is, (θ1_i, θ2_j) = (i·Δθ, j·Δθ). We then converted these joint angles into the ordinary x, y position of the arm tip. When Δθ is small, this would produce an impractically large number of points. So we limited the points to a set workspace (−0.3 < x < 0.3, 0.2 < y < 0.5 m, with the shoulder joint at (0,0)). Only points inside this workspace were included in the training grid.

Cartesian Space Grid Points: This works the same way as the joint-space method, but the points are picked at fixed steps directly in the ordinary x, y workspace. This method is commonly used in training experiments with non-human primates.

Random Grid Points: The starting and target positions are picked at random within the workspace.

In the last two methods, because points are picked directly in the workspace, some locations may be impossible for the arm model to reach. For these points, we had to solve the inverse kinematics, which means working backward from the arm tip's position to find the joint angles. Points that gave joint angles outside the allowed range were thrown out. In this study, we trained the models only on the joint-space grid-point task. We then used the Cartesian space and random point tasks to test whether the trained models had gained the general ability to move from any starting point to any target in the workspace.

2.2.3. The Experimental Tasks

Center-out (CO) task: The center-out design is one of the most common setups in motor control research. It has a central starting point (x, y) and a set of targets spread evenly around a circle centered on that point, with a radius l and an angular separation Δθ. So the task is fully described by these three settings. In our version, Δθ was fixed at 45°. We trained two versions. A single-task model (CO Single) used one fixed set of settings. A multi-task model (CO Multi) was trained on several sets of settings, combining 4 different starting point locations with 3 target distances.

Random target touch (RTT) task: We used a continuous random target task. At the start of each trial, a starting point and a target appear at random locations within the workspace. When the arm reaches a target, the next target appears right away. All targets stay within the workspace, and the distance between one target and the next ranges from 0.05 m to 0.15 m. The arm must start the next movement without delay, so the arm keeps moving throughout the trial.

Double-reach (DR) task: The DR task extends the CO task. It has a fixed central starting point and two targets spread evenly around the circle. Unlike the RTT task, it is a sequential task: both targets appear at the same time, at the start of the trial. After the "GO" cue, the model must make two reaches one after the other, from the center to the first target and then from the first target to the second, with no further task instructions. Because two target positions arrive at once, we widened the task network's input layer from 4 to 6 numbers.

2.2.4. How We Trained the Model

We trained the RNN controller to make point-to-point reaches using supervised learning, which means learning from correct answers. Training had two main phases. (1) In a first "growing up" phase, the model learned basic control of a single reach. In this phase, all settings were trained, both the RNN controller and the task network (Figure 2B). (2) In a second, fine-tuned phase, the model trained on specific tasks. Here the RNN was frozen, and only the task network's settings were updated (Figure 2C).

Reaching Model Training: We first trained newly started RNN models on a general reaching task. In each simulated trial, the model had to move the arm tip from a random starting position to a random target position, both picked evenly from the joint space of the arm model. To stop the model from moving ahead of the cue, we used catch trials. In 50% of trials, no "GO" cue was given. In the valid trials, the "GO" cue came at a random time between 100 ms and 300 ms after the trial began.

Loss Function: We trained the model with a combined loss function designed to shape realistic, efficient movements. The total loss L for a batch of trials was the average over time steps S of a loss Lt for each time step:

L = (Σ_{t=1}^{S} Lt)/S, Lt = λpos L_t^pos + λhold L_t^hold + λtraj L_t^traj + λvel L_t^vel + λj L_t^j + λm L_t^m

The main parts were:

Position Loss (L_t^pos): The L1 norm (the sum of the absolute differences) between the actual arm tip position x_t and the target position x_t*. Before the "GO" cue, the target was the starting position; after it, the target was the final goal position.

Hold Loss (L_t^hold): The squared norm of the arm tip's position before the "GO" cue, which penalized any movement during the preparation period.

Trajectory Loss (L_t^traj): The squared error against an ideal minimum-jerk path during movement.

Velocity Loss (L_t^vel): The squared error against an ideal minimum-jerk speed profile during movement.

Jerk Loss (L_t^j): The squared norm of the arm tip's jerk (the third derivative of position), which encouraged smooth, bell-shaped speed profiles.

Muscle Activity Loss (L_t^m): Penalized the sum of squared muscle forces and their derivatives, which encouraged low-energy muscle activity that did not wobble.

Optimization Details: We trained the models on an NVIDIA RTX 5070Ti computer using the Adam optimizer, a popular method for adjusting a network's settings step by step. The learning rate, which sets how big each step is, is given in the training settings. We clipped the gradients, the signals that tell the network how to change each setting, to a maximum norm of 1.0 to keep training stable. After each step, we enforced certain design rules (for example, sparse connectivity, where each neuron connects to only a few others) using a connectivity constraint method. Training usually lasted 20,000 batches in the basic phase. We recorded the loss parts throughout training to check that it was settling down. Table 2 lists the detailed settings.

2.3. Measuring and Analyzing the Data

2.3.1. Preparing the Data

The neural data from the CO task were recorded in the motor cortex (M1) and in the dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), a brain region that helps plan movements, using Utah array electrodes [52]. These are grids of tiny electrodes placed in the brain. We chose five sessions from Monkey C. Each session had on average 60.0 ± 11.78 units (recording sites, each picking up the activity of a nerve cell) and 118.4 ± 16.86 trials. We also chose five sessions from Monkey M, each with on average 40.8 ± 8.52 units and 210.4 ± 5.31 trials. The neural data from the RTT task were also recorded in M1 and PMd with Utah array electrodes [53,54]. We chose one M1 session from Monkey M, with 61 units and 140 trials. The DR task data came from an NKT dataset [46], with 118 units and 739 trials.

We sorted the raw spike counts into non-overlapping time bins, 30 ms long for the CO task and 10 ms long for the RTT and DR tasks, lined up with the events of each trial. For each neuron, we first took the square root of the binned counts to make their spread more even. We then smoothed the time series by sliding a one-dimensional Gaussian kernel (standard deviation σ = 50 ms) along it. We left out neurons whose average firing rate was below 1 Hz across the whole recording session.

To study how the neural activity differed between conditions, we built trial-averaged firing rate matrices for set time windows. For the movement-related analyses that this study focuses on, we took the neural activity from a 1000 ms window starting 500 ms before movement began in the CO task. We then resampled the activity to 10 ms using cubic spline interpolation, a smooth way of estimating values between points. For the DR task, we took the activity from a 2300 ms window starting 1300 ms before the first movement began. Within this window, we calculated the trial-averaged firing rates for each reach condition (for example, each target direction).

For the RTT task, averaging over trials did not work, because the trials were so different from one another. Each trial contained a different number of reaches, with different target locations and different lengths of time. To make the data comparable, we picked out only trials with exactly four reaches. We then lined up the neural activity of each trial using a fixed time window, set by the shortest total length of time seen across all the chosen trials.

Finally, we applied a "soft" normalization to the firing rate matrix F ∈ R^(n×(c·t)), averaged over conditions and time. Here n is the number of neurons, c the number of conditions, and t the number of time bins per condition. We normalized each neuron's activity by its firing rate range across all conditions and time points, plus a constant offset of 5 Hz: f_norm = f/(range(f) + 5). We then mean-centered the normalized rates for each neuron, so that each neuron's data had an average of 0. The final data matrix X was ready for the next steps, which reduced the data to fewer dimensions or compared how similar the data were.

2.3.2. Analyzing the Activity of Whole Groups of Neurons

To picture the activity of whole groups of neurons, we used dimensionality reduction methods, including principal component analysis (PCA) and jPCA [13]. These methods squeeze many measurements into a few main directions that capture most of the variation. jPCA describes how the neural state vector x(t) changes over time and across conditions using a linear dynamical system: ẋ(t) = M x(t). We required the matrix M to be skew-symmetric, which means M^T = −M. This makes M capture only the swirling, rotating flow in state space, the pattern of activity that goes round in cycles.

Before running jPCA, we projected the neural data (the firing rates of n neurons) onto their first 12 principal components. This cut down the number of dimensions and focused on the strong signals shared by the group of neurons. We ran the analysis on a 500 ms window from 280 ms before to 220 ms after movement began, a period when the neural activity changes a lot. Unlike the usual use of jPCA, we did not subtract the average activity across conditions. This let us compare directly the cycles found by jPCA with the changes over time in our RNN models, which we studied as linearized around fixed points. As summary measures, we used how well the fit matched and the eigenvalues of the fitted M matrix, which show how fast the cycles repeat.

2.3.3. Canonical Correlation Analysis

To see how similar the pattern of which states the network visits is across different models, we used a two-step method that reduces the data to fewer dimensions and then lines them up [44]. First, we estimated the low-dimensional hidden activity of the recorded neurons in each session. For each session, we applied PCA to X to define a low-dimensional neural manifold, a flat surface that captures the main patterns of activity, using the leading m principal components (neural modes, where m = 10). We then projected the full neural activity onto these neural modes, giving the hidden activity matrix L ∈ R^(m×T).

Next, we used canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to line up the hidden activity from pairs of sessions, across different individuals doing similar behaviors. CCA finds the linear transformations that make the two sets of hidden signals as closely correlated as possible. The resulting correlations are called canonical correlations (CCs). We used CCA to calculate a CC score on 10 principal components. We then calculated the Area Under the Curve (AUC) of each CCA curve to measure how similar the two were.

To measure uncertainty, we used a session-level bootstrap. For each condition, we drew B = 10,000 bootstrap samples by resampling the N sessions with replacement, meaning a session could be picked more than once. We recalculated the average AUC for each sample. We took the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the 95% confidence interval, the range that should contain the true value 95% of the time. For comparisons between a model and monkey data, we calculated the paired bootstrap difference Δ = AUC_model − AUC_monkey over the same resampled sessions. The two-sided p-value was defined as twice the share of bootstrap differences with the opposite sign to the observed average difference [55].

2.3.4. Comparing How Activity Changes Over Time

To measure carefully how similar the internal computing processes are in how they change over time, we used dynamical similarity analysis (DSA) [45]. DSA compares the dynamical systems behind the observed time series, not just the shapes of the activity. It has two stages.

(1) We extracted a globally linear description of the underlying nonlinear system using Koopman operator theory and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD). Koopman operator theory lets a complicated nonlinear system be described by a simple linear one. DMD finds the best-fitting linear operator A that moves the state forward in time: x_(t+1) ≈ A x_t. This operator captures the essential features of how the system changes.

(2) We compared the resulting transition operators using an extension of statistical shape analysis, a method for comparing shapes, adapted for vector fields. We lined up the two DMD operators as well as possible and then calculated the Procrustes distance between them, a measure of how far apart two shapes are. This gives a single DSA score, where lower values mean the two systems are more alike in how they change over time. In other words, the two systems are closer to being topologically conjugate, meaning they follow the same kind of flow.

(9) DSA = ‖K̃x − Q K̃y Q^T‖_F / (‖K̃x‖_F + ‖K̃y‖_F),

where K̃x and K̃y are the reduced DMD operators and Q is the best orthogonal alignment matrix, the rotation and scaling that lines the two operators up best. Lower DSA scores mean more similar dynamics.

We measured uncertainty with the same session-level bootstrap (B = 10,000, 95% percentile confidence interval). Because different conditions sometimes had different numbers of sessions, we used unpaired bootstrapping for DSA comparisons across conditions, resampling each group separately.

2.3.5. Testing Our Hypotheses

We used the Friedman test as the overall test of whether the k conditions differ in their typical values across sessions. The Friedman test is a non-parametric repeated-measures analysis of variance, which compares several conditions measured on the same sessions without assuming the data follow a bell-shaped curve. If all conditions come from the same distribution, the Friedman statistic follows a χ² (chi-squared) distribution with k − 1 degrees of freedom. We also report the Iman–Davenport correction, which improves the test's behavior when there are few sessions [56].

We compared pairs of conditions afterward using the bootstrap percentile methods described above. For the five model-versus-monkey comparisons, we corrected all p-values with the Holm–Bonferroni step-down procedure [57]. This adjustment keeps the family-wise error rate at α = 0.05, so that the chance of a false alarm somewhere among the five comparisons stays at 5%.

For each model-versus-monkey comparison, we report the bootstrap average difference Δ and its 95% confidence interval. How far the model strays from the monkey baseline can be read directly from Δ (for CCA-AUC) or the raw DSA score (for DSA), both on their original measurement scales. We carried out all statistical analyses with custom Python scripts (Python 3.11) built on NumPy [58], SciPy [59], and scikit-learn [60]. Unless we say otherwise, we report bootstrap confidence intervals and hypothesis tests at the 95% confidence level, and we controlled for multiple comparisons with the Holm–Bonferroni procedure [57].

3. Results

3.1. How Well the Pre-Trained Model Reaches, and How Its Activity Behaves

We first limited the arm's reach to a workspace 0.05–0.35 m across. We then built a set of reaching tasks on a grid of points in joint space, which means the grid is laid out over the angles of the arm's joints rather than over positions in the room. We made three versions of this grid, which we call dense, moderate and sparse. The dense grid had 25 points, the moderate grid had 15, and the sparse grid had eight. The points were spaced 15°, 20° and 25° apart in joint angle, respectively. We trained each model for 20,000 epochs, where one epoch is one full pass through the training examples.

Our aim was to give the single-reach (SR) model a basic reaching skill. Once the model is told the position of a target, it should move the hand of the simulated arm, from any starting position, to that target. The path it takes should closely follow the minimum-jerk trajectory, the smooth, natural path of reaching.

After training, we picked a smaller set of hand positions to look at more closely. We studied the RNN's activity for every path that started at one position in this set and ended at another, trying every possible pair (Figure 3A). To make sense of this, we used principal component analysis (PCA). This method squeezes many measurements into a few main directions, called principal components, that capture most of the differences between them. The top 10 of these directions captured more than 90% of all the variation in the activity.

For each set of reaches (shown as solid or dashed lines), the network's activity at the end of the preparation phase kept the same shape as the real positions. It matched the target positions (squares) or the starting positions (triangles) (Figure 3B). We also looked at pairs of reaches that swap the start and the target. Their paths through the network's activity were mirror images across the center. This shows that swapping the start and target sends the network's starting state in opposite directions during preparation. During the movement itself, the activity then moved along directions that were at right angles to the preparation directions (Figure 3C).

Figure 3

How the reaching model performs and how its activity changes. (A–C) A chosen set of target pairs from the joint-space grid task. The panels show the hand's path, the network's activity during preparation, and the network's activity during movement, each in a 3D space of principal components (PC). Numbers and colors mark particular targets. Solid and dashed lines show the outward and return reaches for the same pair. (E,G) Hand paths in the room-position grid task and the random target grid task. (D–H) Cross-correlation scores for paths and speeds, and the final hand errors, for all three task types and all three model types. *: p<0.05; **: p<0.01; ***: p<0.001; ns, not significant.

Figure 3D shows how well the models trained on the three grid densities did on the task they were trained on. The models trained on the 25-point and 15-point grids both performed strongly. Their tracking errors and hand errors were significantly lower than those of the model trained on the eight-point grid. To test whether the models could handle new situations, we then tried the three SR models on room-position grid points spaced at different distances (Figure 3E) and on randomly chosen start and target positions (Figure 3G). The models performed strongly, in line with how they had done during training (Figure 3F,G). Taken together, these results for behavior and for the network's activity show that the SR model has learned to produce realistic arm paths across the whole workspace. It does so in a way that closely matches the patterns seen in the real motor cortex.

3.2. The Pre-Trained Model Matches the Real Brain's Activity Patterns and Changes More Closely

Once we had checked the SR models, we compared their activity with real recordings from the motor cortex. For this we used a standard center-out (CO) task, in which the animal reaches from a central point to targets spread around it in eight directions (Figure 4A). Because every reach in this task goes from the same center to a target around the edge, the SR model could carry it out zero-shot. This means it did so without any extra training or adjustment of its settings (Figure 4B).

Figure 4

How well the model matches real data in the center-out (CO) task. (A) Diagram of the 8-direction CO task. (B) Hand paths for a set of CO reaches. (C) Activity of four typical network units, each tuned in a different way, like real nerve cells. Each profile matches the reach of the same color in (B). (D) Rotating patterns in the network's activity during movement, found with jPCA. Each rotating path matches the reach of the same color in (B). (E) Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) scores comparing all candidate models with real recordings from Monkey C. The curves show how the canonical correlation (CC) scores with the network's main activity patterns are spread out for each model type. The area under each curve (AUC) summarizes it, as shown in the legend. (F) The same as (E) for Monkey M.

In the CO task, the activity of individual network units varied a great deal, and it closely matched well-known features of the real motor cortex (Figure 4C). Node 100 was strongly tuned only during preparation, and this tuning collapsed once the movement began. Node 32 stayed quiet during preparation but became strongly active during movement. Node 13 was tuned to the same direction in both periods. Node 4 was active in both periods, but its preferred direction flipped after the "GO" signal. We also used jPCA, a method that finds the main patterns of change in a network's activity, on the activity during movement. It revealed the typical rotating patterns seen in groups of nerve cells in the motor cortex (Figure 4D). Together, these findings confirm in a general, descriptive way that the SR model's activity changes in the same way as the real brain's.

To test this with numbers, we asked whether the pre-trained SR model is a better stand-in for the motor cortex than models trained only on the CO task. For a fair comparison, we trained one model type only on the standard CO task (we call it CO Single). We also changed the task settings step by step, namely the central starting position and the reaching distance, to build a collection of 12 different CO tasks. We trained a second model type on all of them (CO Multi). We then used canonical correlation analysis (CCA, Method 2.3.3) to line up the network's activity space with the activity space of the real recordings from both Monkey M and Monkey C. CCA finds the main patterns in the network's activity and measures how closely each one lines up with the main patterns in the brain recordings. We then worked out how the canonical correlation (CC) scores were spread across different recording sessions, both for the animal-to-animal comparison and for the animal-to-model comparison. We summarized each spread with the area under the curve (AUC).

As Figure 4E shows, all models matched the baseline very well in the first three main activity patterns. The baseline was set by comparing different recording sessions of Monkey C. From the fourth pattern onward, the differences became significant. In terms of the AUC scores, the SR models always did better than the CO models. Within each group, the models trained on more data performed better. A simple test that removed parts of the model showed that this result does not depend on the size of the RNN (Figure 5). For both monkeys, the CCA-AUC scores ranked the models in the same order. We checked this with a Friedman test, which asks whether several models rank consistently across many comparisons. The ranking was statistically significant for Monkey C (χ2=36.6, p<0.001) and for Monkey M (χ2=22.5, p<0.001). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. For p<0.001, that would happen less than 0.1% of the time. The SR models always matched the real data more closely than the CO models (Table 3).

Figure 5

We also used a second measure, the distance of similarity (DSA). It measures how far apart two systems' rules for changing over time are, after those rules have been simplified into a linear form. A lower DSA score means a closer match. This measure gave exactly the same ranking. The SR Dense model matched the monkey's activity changes most closely. All seven model types had significantly different DSA scores (Friedman test, χ2=24.0, p<0.001 for Monkey C; χ2=23.7, p<0.001 for Monkey M). Every pair of models differed significantly (bootstrap difference test, Holm-corrected p<0.001) for both monkeys. The one exception was CO Single versus DR Multi in Monkey M (p=0.516).

The DSA also showed that the SR models form their own family. This family is significantly closer to the real activity changes than the CO and DR models are (Kruskal–Wallis test, H=19.9, p<0.001). The average DSA across the families was 0.045±0.010 for SR and 0.076±0.014 for CO. Within the SR family, the more sparse the grid, the worse the match: DSA was 0.032 for Dense, 0.047 for Moderate and 0.052 for Sparse. This suggests that more connections between the network's units capture the rich timing of the brain's activity better.

The CCA-AUC and DSA results point to the same conclusion. The SR model, especially the dense version, matches the patterns and changes of the real brain's activity more closely. This advantage is statistically solid across two monkeys and several measures that complement each other. These results show that even when it does only the CO task, the SR model's activity patterns and changes were nearly identical to the real data. They were also significantly better than those of models trained only on the CO task. The CO models may have learned only the most basic information the task needs, such as the first three main activity patterns found by canonical correlation (CC). The activity in the higher patterns likely holds richer information. The CO Multi model also did better than the CO Single model. Together, these findings suggest that models trained on a single task mainly learn the rules of that task. Training data that cover a wider range lets a model learn abilities linked to specific motor control, which makes it more like the real data.

3.3. The Fine-Tuned SR Model Matches the Real Brain's Activity Changes More Closely in the Random Target Task

Next, we moved on to a harder task that demands more from the network: the random target task (RTT). It directly tests whether the network can produce smooth, one after another, movements. In this task, a new target appears the moment the animal has successfully reached the previous one. So the model must quickly switch from stopping one reach to starting the next, keeping the behavior flowing (Figure 6A). To do this, we set up each trial with three targets shown one after another. Importantly, we froze all the internal connections between the network's units in the pre-trained SR models. We adjusted only the settings of the task network layer, the part that turns the sequence of instructions into activity in the existing network. For a fair baseline, we also trained an RTT model from scratch, using exactly the same design.

Figure 6

How the model performs in the random target task (RTT). (A) Diagram of the RTT task. (B) A typical hand path from one continuous RTT trial. (C) The speed profile for the path shown in (B).

After training, all the candidate networks learned the sequence task well. Figure 6B,C show typical hand paths and speed profiles from a single trial of the fine-tuned SR Dense model. The RTT task is random, so the targets and the length of each reach varied a lot from trial to trial. Because of this, the usual way of measuring match, which averages over many trials, works less well than DSA. The RTT model trained from scratch matched the real activity changes less closely than the fine-tuned SR models (Table 4). These results support the reasonable conclusion that the SR model has built a strong structure for changing over time. This structure closely matches the basic ways the real motor cortex computes while it carries out continuous movement.

3.4. Moving in Sequence Needs Different Underlying Ways of Computing

Finally, we turned to a more complex but more common behavior: moving in sequence. This is different from the continuous-reach task (RTT) we studied before. In a sequence, the subject must name all the next targets before it starts moving, and it must carry out the whole series in one unbroken chain of actions. This closely matches the kinds of movement people use in daily life. We studied the simplest form of this: a double-reach (DR) task (Figure 7A). As in the CO task, both targets for the two reaches in a row appeared at the same time during preparation, rather than the second target appearing only after the first movement. The network then had to make two reaches one after the other during movement.

To handle two target positions at once, we widened the input layer of the task network to six, and left all other settings unchanged. Following the same CO training plan, we changed the central starting position, the reaching distance and the angular spacing of the outer targets step by step. This gave us a collection of 16 different DR task setups. We then fine-tuned each pre-trained SR model, both on a single task and on many tasks. Together with two baseline DR models trained from scratch, we tested eight model types in total.

Figure 7

How the models match in the double-reach (DR) task. (A) Diagram of the DR task. (B) Hand paths for a set of DR tasks. Paths of different colors go to different second targets. (C) Speed profile for the paths shown in (B). (D) CCA curves and AUC for each model type.

After training, all the groups of networks learned the DR task well. Figure 7B shows typical hand paths to the same starting targets, and Figure 7C shows the matching speed profiles. We then used CCA and DSA on all the models. Surprisingly, the DR task flipped the patterns we had seen in both the CO and RTT tasks. The model trained from scratch matched the real recordings significantly more closely, both in its activity patterns and in how its activity changes (Figure 7D). The DSA showed the same result. For SR Single the scores were 0.0999, 0.0668 and 0.0967, and for SR Multi they were 0.0967, 0.0756 and 0.0836. For DR Single the score was 0.0493, and for DR Multi it was 0.0246.

This unexpected difference suggests that a single reach and a double reach may be two fundamentally different basic movement skills. So the ability to join two separate movements into one joined-up sequence may depend on basic, built-in ways of computing in the motor circuits. At the same time, the DR Multi model did better than the DR Single model. This supports what we saw earlier in the CO task: training data that cover a wider range and more variety push the network's internal patterns closer to how the real brain works.

To check further that the SR and DR models really differ in how their activity changes, we ran a reverse-transfer experiment. We fine-tuned the DR model trained from scratch on the standard CO task. We brought the task network's input width back to four and froze the internal connections between the network's units. Notably, this fine-tuned DR model matched both monkeys' activity changes least well. Interestingly, the DR Multi model, which had matched the real data most closely during the DR task, now showed the largest difference from the real data when it was limited to a single reach. Its scores were 0.076 for Monkey C and 0.081 for Monkey M, compared with 0.088 for Monkey C and 0.0918 for Monkey M for DR Multi. This shortfall shows that the DR model uses a fundamentally different way of computing from the SR model. It gives strong evidence that single movements and sequences of several movements are controlled by separate basic movement skills.
parts.discussion:
4. Discussion

In this study, we built a reaching model that imitates the way an animal moves. We first trained an RNN to control a computer model of an arm with muscles and joints across a wide area of space. This gave the network a kind of "motor experience", a set of basic movement skills that an animal builds up as it grows. That experience shapes the network's internal workings in ways that mirror how a real brain develops. The trained controller can then quickly adapt to new kinds of tasks by fine-tuning only the layer that receives the task instructions. Further results showed that this pretraining leads to patterns of activity and changes over time that more closely resemble those seen in the brain's own nerve circuits. Finally, our results suggest that the ability to join single reaches into a pair of reaches, one after the other, may depend on ways of computing that are built into the motor cortex itself.

4.1. Pretraining as a Computer Version of Learning to Move as We Grow Up

In recent years, more and more studies have trained RNNs to learn basic movement building blocks (motor primitives), with the aim of helping the networks handle new situations better [21,61,62,63,64]. However, these studies usually relied on fairly simple tasks, such as reaching from the center of a screen out to one of eight directions. They also needed extra methods to make the networks work on other kinds of movement. Examples include searching for a good starting state, or adjusting how strongly the network responds to its inputs (gain modulation).

In our work, we trained the model on a grid-point reaching task, where the targets are points on a grid. Our goal was to let the model acquire basic reaching ability from training examples that were larger in scale and more widely spread out. From the point of view of machine learning, this step can be seen as pretraining, a strategy that is now widely used in artificial intelligence. Pretraining methods have advanced quickly in large artificial neural networks, especially in areas such as understanding human language and recognizing images. They have shown that exposure to broad and varied collections of data lets models build up rich knowledge that carries over to new situations.

Large language models are a good example. They learn on their own from huge amounts of text that has no labels, picking out statistical regularities and the chances of one word following another. This gives them high-quality starting settings, a better place to begin when they are later fine-tuned for a specific subject, so they settle on good answers faster and use fewer computing resources [65,66,67]. At the same time, a small number of studies have pointed out that these large models share some features with real brains [68,69]. In computational neuroscience, however, pretraining has been used in only a very small number of studies [70]. Our work extends this idea to modeling how the brain controls movement. We show that pretraining an RNN on a wide range of reaching skills makes its internal workings much more similar to the activity recorded from the motor cortex.

We also found that, in both the center-out (CO) and double-reach (DR) tasks, the versions trained on several tasks at once always did better than the versions trained on just one task. This fits the basic logic of pretraining. By first exposing the network to a wide range of movements, set up in many different ways, the network is pushed to build general movement knowledge and basic patterns of change over time before it adapts to the limits of any particular task. Our grid-point pretraining task is a large-scale, systematic way of building these general abilities. Training on several tasks, on the other hand, lets the network share what it has learned and reuse features across tasks within a closely related family of behaviors. So the two ideas share the same underlying mechanism: reusing what has already been learned.

In other words, training on several tasks can be thought of as a kind of weak pretraining. Because it has no separate, step-by-step pretraining stage, it reuses knowledge and learns the target task at the same time. As a result, its training intensity, the range of behaviors it covers, and the highest level of generalization it can reach are naturally lower than those of a dedicated pretraining stage inspired by how animals develop. In the end, training on several tasks works as a light, side-by-side warm-up, not as a full foundation for development.

When RNNs are used to simulate the brain, pretraining can be seen as a computer version of development. It imitates the years of sensing and moving that shape how the connections and workings of the brain's nerve circuits come to be. In both the CO and the random target touch (RTT) tasks, the pre-trained RNN showed patterns of activity and changes over time that matched recordings from monkeys more closely than networks trained from scratch. This suggests that pretraining encourages the RNN to use ways of computing that have been fine-tuned by evolution and development. These may include organizing its states efficiently, coping well with noise, and being able to reuse existing patterns of change for new tasks.

By starting from a pre-trained network and then fine-tuning it on specific tasks, researchers can more clearly see how task-specific fine-tuning changes the patterns that were already there. This is easier than studying networks whose patterns have been shaped mainly by a single task. This approach fits recent directions in neuroscience on "meta-learning" [71], which is learning how to learn, and on "foundation models" [72], which are large models trained on many kinds of data. Adapting one shared network to many different experimental conditions makes it possible to compare tasks cleanly and to pick out the parts of the brain's workings that stay the same across tasks.

4.2. A Series of Movements Is Fundamentally Different from a Single Movement

It is worth noting that in the double-reach task, the pre-trained model did much worse at matching the patterns of activity than the double-reach model trained from scratch, even though it had a rich set of single-reach skills. This is the opposite of what we saw in the earlier results. One explanation is that a series of movements is not simply a chain of separate movement commands, each triggered by outside task instructions. Instead, it may need a different kind of internal workings that brings several goals in space together into one joined-up movement plan before the movement is carried out.

Evidence from recordings of nerve cells supports this view. It shows that motor cortex nerve cells can represent a whole series of movements as one unit, rather than as separate pieces. This explanation also fits the theory of dynamic primitives, which proposes that single point-to-point movements and series of combined actions belong to fundamentally different classes of basic movement, each with its own way of being controlled [73].

Studies of human brains using fMRI, a method that shows which brain areas are active, further support this separation. In the primary motor cortex (M1), the main area that sends movement commands, the activity patterns for a series of movements can be fully explained by adding together the patterns for the single movements that make it up. In contrast, the premotor and parietal areas, which help plan and coordinate movement, carry real information about the series as a whole, beyond what the single movements add up to [74,75]. What these areas represent also changes over time: while planning, each area encodes separate features, but while the movement is being carried out, they encode the movements together. This change happens only in series of movements and not in single reaches [76].

Studies in monkeys other than humans have shown that the activity in M1 and in the dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) before a movement can reflect the structure of the whole series. They have also shown that the movements coming next affect how nerve cells encode the task, and that the encoding patterns shift while the movement is being carried out [46]. When looking at groups of nerve cells together, the brain starts preparing for the second movement while the first one is still being carried out [47]. This ability to join movements together and prepare the next one while the current one is happening may depend on particular circuit designs or particular patterns of change over time. Several studies of computer models have shown that networks with several time scales [48], networks with metastable attractors, which are states the network tends to settle into for a while before switching [49], and loops between the thalamus and the cortex [50] all help produce series of movements.

The fine-tuned double-reach model also did worse than the single-reach (SR) model when we tested it on the center-out task. This suggests that future research should explore structured pretraining, meaning pretraining designed around the task, for example by choosing which tasks to include or by designing a learning curriculum. Such pretraining could better capture the layered, step-by-step way that animals build up natural movement skills.

This view matters for both neuroscience and neural engineering. If producing a series of movements is indeed a core skill of the motor cortex, then brain–machine interfaces designed to control a series of movements may benefit from decoders, the parts that turn brain signals into commands, that make use of these built-in patterns of change, rather than relying only on outside cues. In the same way, approaches to rehabilitation after brain injury could aim to strengthen or restore the brain's own ways of sequencing movements within its motor circuits.

4.3. RNNs Have Advantages for Modeling the Motor Cortex and Controlling an Arm with Muscles and Joints

In this study, we asked the RNN to control a computer model of an arm with muscles and joints, rather than simply outputting movement paths, speeds, or muscle electrical signals (electromyographic signals). In recent years, more and more studies have used arm models to make their simulations as realistic as possible [37,39]. Controlling a device with its own physical limits and behavior is harder than directly producing movement values, and it leads to very different activity in the network. Earlier modeling studies have shown that even controlling devices with different features, such as an arm versus an eye, leads to clearly different patterns of change over time in the network [38]. From the point of view of embodied intelligence, intelligence does not sit inside the brain on its own. It arises from the back-and-forth between the body and the world, especially for motor intelligence [77], where physically handling things is crucial.

According to optimal feedback control (OFC) theory, the brain keeps internal models, which are mental copies of how its body works. These models can predict what the senses will tell us as we move, and they can combine delayed, noisy sensory feedback (for example, from sight or from the sense of where the body is) to form more accurate and timely estimates of where the limb is right now [78]. To study closed-loop control, where the brain keeps correcting its movements using feedback, a model of muscles and joints adds realistic delays, noise, nonlinearities (behaviors that do not simply scale up in proportion), and redundancy (more muscles than are strictly needed to move the arm). All of these are key factors that shape how the brain controls movement. Training an RNN to control such a system helps it develop sturdy controllers that work in many situations, with properties similar to the way biological motor control adapts and copes with faults.

Combining RNNs with models of arms with muscles and joints gives us a powerful way to simulate how the motor cortex brings together its built-in patterns of change with learning for specific tasks. This approach not only makes the models perform better and match the brain more closely, but also gives us a platform for producing ideas that can be tested about how the brain adapts movement, how it combines skills, and how feedback shapes the activity of the cortex. Future research should extend this approach to more complex tasks, richer sensory inputs, and other ways of learning, such as reinforcement learning. This would help close the gap between artificial and biological motor intelligence, and would provide models and theoretical designs for the field of robot control that copies the brain.

4.4. Limitations and Future Work

Our study has several limitations that future work should address.

Models of muscles and joints. Our model is a flat, two-jointed arm moved by six muscles (called RigidTendonArm26). This gives a realistic basis for closed-loop control using sensory feedback, but it is a big simplification of the human upper arm. The human upper arm has more than thirty muscles, with complex arrangements: muscle fibers run at different angles to the muscle (pennation angles), there are different types of muscle fibers, and some muscles cross more than one joint. Earlier work has shown that adding more detail about the body's mechanics can change the ways of controlling movement that models learn [42,79]. We do not yet know how much extra muscle detail would change our conclusions about how closely the network matches the brain and about basic movement building blocks. Adding more complete models of muscles and joints, with more degrees of freedom (for example, a wrist and a hand), would test how widely our findings apply and let us study dexterous manipulation, the kind of skilled hand movements used to handle objects.

Delays in sensory feedback. We set the delays for visual and body-position feedback to zero during both training and testing. In real biological motor control, feedback is delayed by about 50–150 ms for vision and 30–50 ms for the sense of body position. A large body of work has shown that the brain makes up for these delays using internal forward models, which predict what will happen next. These are likely carried out in the circuit between the brain and the cerebellum, a brain region that helps coordinate movement [80,81]. To make up for delays well, a system needs at least three things: a memory buffer that stores copies of the commands the brain sends out (efference copies), a state observer that estimates the current state, and a predictor that simulates what will happen next [81]. Patients with damage to the cerebellum show a larger lag in their feedback control, which fits with losing this predictive ability [82]. Models trained without delays may learn fundamentally different ways of controlling movement, reacting to what has happened rather than predicting what will happen. This could affect how well their activity matches the delay-aware circuits of the brain. Adding realistic delays in future work would test whether our model develops forward-model-like calculations on its own, and whether this makes it even more similar to neural recordings.

Scaling up to complex behaviors. We tested our model on reaching and on pairs of reaches, which is only a small part of the range of movement skills. Scaling up to more complex behaviors, built in layers, such as using a tool in several steps, coordinating the whole body, or interacting with objects that can be moved, is unlikely to work with an RNN that has a single time scale and learns only from correct answers. Earlier work suggests that reliable sequencing and layered control need dedicated mechanisms for switching between patterns of change [50] and neural activity that runs on several time scales [48]. Designs that split the work into separate parts for encoding, scheduling, and carrying out movement have shown that what is learned for two-step movements can be combined to handle longer sequences that were never trained [83]. Future work should explore whether adding such design features to our pretraining approach lets the model learn a wider range of complex behaviors.

Neural recordings. Our comparisons with the brain are based on a small set of recordings: 10 sessions from two monkeys for the center-out task, one session for the random target touch task, and one dataset for the double-reach task (118 nerve cells). Methods that compare the overall patterns of change, such as CCA (canonical correlation analysis, which finds the patterns in two sets of data that line up most closely) and dynamical similarity analysis (which measures how closely the patterns of change match), are fairly robust to differences between sessions and between animals [44,84]. Even so, more recordings from more animals, more tasks, and more recording methods would give stronger support for how well the model matches the brain and would reveal ways in which it might fail. In particular, recording at the same time from several brain areas (M1, PMd, the supplementary motor area (SMA), and the parietal cortex) while the animal does the task would allow richer comparisons with the spread-out patterns in our model.

Analysis of the RNN's activity and design. So far, we have mostly treated the pre-trained RNN as a black box. We used CCA and dynamical similarity analysis to compare the patterns of change in the network's hidden states with neural recordings, without trying to work out step by step how the network actually does its computing. A well-developed set of tools exists for opening this black box. Fixed-point analysis finds attractor structures and slow manifolds, which are states the network tends to settle into or move along slowly [29]. Jacobian linearization describes how the network's inputs and outputs are linked near those settled states. Low-dimensional projection methods, such as demixed PCA [85], separate the parts of the network's activity that represent the task from the parts that represent the task's settings.

Applying these tools to our model could show whether pretraining creates patterns of change, such as rotational dynamics [20] or low-rank connectivity structures [86] (a particular kind of organized wiring), that mirror those seen in the motor cortex, and how these differ from the model trained from scratch. Earlier work has shown that RNNs trained separately on the same task end up with the same universal patterns of change [87], and that learning in the motor cortex involves recombining existing patterns rather than creating entirely new activity [88]. Checking whether our pre-trained model's activity follows these principles would make our approach much easier to interpret in terms of the brain. Future work should also look at how the pre-trained network flexibly combines its different parts across tasks [30], and whether its wiring shows the low-rank separability that is thought to underlie computing in the brain's own nerve circuits [86,89].

RNNs built with biological limits. A stronger way to build in biology is connectome-constrained modeling, which uses measured maps of the brain's wiring to decide whether each connection between nerve cells (each synapse) exists, and how strong it is. This approach was first developed for the visual system of the fruit fly Drosophila, where a complete wiring map at the level of single synapses is available. It has shown that networks built on the wiring map of the fly's optic lobe can accurately predict neural responses across dozens of experimental conditions using only a handful of free settings [90]. Theory has shown that wiring maps alone are often not enough to pin down how a network behaves: a fixed wiring map allows many different patterns of change. Recordings from a small number of nerve cells can break this tie [91].

In the mammalian brain, the MICrONS dataset for the mouse visual cortex combines nearly 12,000 excitatory nerve cells, each with its position, its connections, and its activity. This has made it possible to build RNNs grounded in biology, whose starting settings and layout in space reflect the measured wiring of the cortex. These networks develop a low-entropy, modular, small-world organization, meaning their activity is less random, they are split into groups that work together, and they are tightly linked both within and between groups. They also do better than networks without these limits on tasks that involve making decisions [92]. Adding wiring-map limits to our pretraining approach, even partial ones such as the layout in space or statistics of the wiring patterns, would let us compare the network's learned weights directly with wiring data from the motor cortex. This would connect RNNs that perform tasks with models of the brain's small-scale circuits that are grounded in structure.

Brain–machine interfaces with decoders that use patterns of change. Recurrent neural networks have become a popular design for decoding brain signals recorded inside the cortex in closed-loop brain–machine interfaces. They consistently outperform linear and transformer-based alternatives in real-time tasks that control a finger or a cursor [93,94]. Our pre-trained RNN, whose internal patterns of change already mirror the activity of the motor cortex, could serve as a structured starting point for these decoders, shortening the time needed to tune them and helping them work across different sessions. This adds to recent approaches based on foundation models. NDT3, a Transformer pre-trained on more than 2000 hours of neural spike data from more than 30 monkeys and humans, has shown that large-scale pretraining helps decoding in later stages when the real-world data differ from the training data [95]. Similarly, POSSM combines spike tokenization, which turns spikes into short codes, with recurrent state-space models, and has carried patterns of change across species, from the monkey motor cortex to decoders for human handwriting [96].

Our approach offers a different, hypothesis-driven path. Pretraining in a closed-loop setting, with sensing and moving, may produce patterns that are naturally easier to transfer to decoding the brain, because they reflect the same computing limits that shape real neural activity. Beyond decoding from stored recordings, online RNN approaches such as RONDO improve decoding accuracy by 35–45% over offline methods within real-time limits [97]. This suggests that our RNN, which runs continuously, could be adapted for adaptive, closed-loop brain–computer interface use. RNN decoders have also been used successfully to control both hands from signals recorded inside the cortex in human participants [98], and to decode finger movements smoothly and with high performance, making it possible to control a quadcopter drone in a game in real time [99]. This shows that the approach is mature enough for clinical brain–computer interface use.
